Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do I keep seeing questions, then it asks if it was a useful answer to my question, but those aren’t my questions or my username?
Answer: If you follow a question, Quora will treat it as if it's your question. So if you followed the questions, that's what's going on. If you didn't follow them, then it's probably one of the many Quora bugs. Either it followed them for you spontaneously, or it is otherwise short circuiting and sending you announcements for some other account.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I study data structures to completely understand them? For example, I solved more than 20 problems in DS stack, but after like 5 hours, I almost forgot every solution and the logic to solve it.
Answer: You…solved 20 problems? For real? Then why are you saying that you forgot the solutions? If you knew enough to solve them, then why would you need to memorize the solutions that you produced the first time? Do you actually mean you typed in the solutions for twenty problems? Because typing in solutions that you've Googled is not solving. The goal with data structures and algorithms isn't to memorize. It's too learn and understand. The ultimate goal is to learn to program. Data structures challenges are just a focused way to practice programming. You don't learn to program by memorizing solutions. You learn to program by programming. By writing novel code for any problems you face, and internalizing the strategies. Practice that and you won't need to memorize anything.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do you think engineers, especially software developers, are overpaid?
Answer: Kurt Guntheroth points out that supply and demand puts software developer compensation at exactly the point the market will bear. Which is 100% correct. What confuses me about this question, though, is how the asker could even wonder if we're “overpaid.” What would the criteria be? More money than they want to spend to create their billion dollar app, presumably? But there it is. “Billion dollar.” A software developer has the potential to create software that makes a potentially unlimited amount of money. How can even a half million dollars per year be “too much” when the potential profits from a single developer can be into the millions per year? Why would someone consider a 500% profit on the software developer's services to be overpaid? Either extreme wishful thinking, in the case of person who actually wants a developer to create their million dollar idea for peanuts since they don't have the funding they need to pay for development…or simply raw greed, in the case of the person who is running a company that is making millions, and they resent the need to pay a developer a fair wage for their work. Back to Kurt's point: Not everyone can be a competent software engineer. I suspect that the percentage of the population who has the right aptitude may not be more than a percent. Maybe a tenth of a percent. Probably half or more professional developers don't hit the minimum threshold, are struggling to get by, and will transition to a management role before they're 30. So when someone is genuinely good at software engineering? The supply of such developers is limited by the number of developers with that aptitude, and demand is high because billion dollar apps are a thing, so compensation keeps going up. And from the other side, an engineer's potential for profits for the company hiring them is limited only by the business plan (and savvy) of the company management, and so there is no inherent limit of “value per hour of work” that you'd see in other industries. So no, there's really no such thing as “overpaid” in software engineering. “Underpaid,” however, is endemic.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is the use of learning high level programming language if future generation of computers can be programmed by using human language?
Answer: I answered a very similar question on Quora already: The underlying difficulty of creating software is entirely unrelated to the syntax of any particular programming language. I have to assume that whoever asked this question is imagining something like a computer on Star Trek, where you can just describe something you need, and the computer writes the program for you. Or you ask for a scene on a planet, and it just creates that scene for you. Credit: A very comprehensive and precise spec So, in their head, the asker is imagining describing an app in English, something like: “I want an app that will remind me of any appointments that I have, whether in my Google Calendar or on my office calendar, and it will take voice commands to add items to both calendars. I also want to share my calendar with friends.” I specifically describe an app here that could be developed with the proper team of developers. Even a team of humans would have a hard time with that English sentence, though. Problems: There are many more. But that last point makes a good transition: The real problem is that you need a computer (or a human development team) to ask all of these questions and understand the answers. In other words, the computer needs to be fully as smart as a human. It would need to understand human context, and what a calendar is, and what privacy is, and why some kinds of privacy might be important. And despite all of the recent advances in “AI”, we're actually no closer to “Strong AI,” an AI that thinks and understands like a human, than we were in the 1950s when they thought strong AI was only 20 years away. It's still at least 20 years away. And I wouldn't be surprised that it turns out to be 20 years away 50 years from now. I actually used to be more bullish on strong AI, but I feel the field has been stagnant for 20 years, despite all the advances in machine learning. Until you have strong AI, you will need programmers to do anything that hasn't already been done. There do exist drag-and-drop app creators (written by programmers) that can automate the creation of apps with specific features. Those will certainly get more advanced and capable. But there will always be a need for developers who understand the minutiae of how software works. And that minutiae is the domain of software engineers. Even when they're using increasingly advanced tools to assemble components. Tools that won't look like English in the foreseeable future, because English is terrible for precision specifications, which is what you're really writing when you're creating software. And the hard part is understanding the specifications, not the language. So the very premise of this question is misguided. More recently DALL-E has been giving people the idea that computers are starting to understand us. Nope. As soon as you dig a bit deeper you discover that it ignored half of the things you asked for and didn't quite understand the other half. So stop making excuses that don't have any basis in reality and start learning how to program. Or at least admit to yourself that you just don't feel like it. Making up unsupported reasons to avoid hard work is just a form of lying to yourself. See also: Tim Mensch's answer to In 2018 why are so many people fixated on programming/coding language/careers/minutiae when software engineering and automated code generation have been around for ages and will displace 80% of coding Real Soon Now?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do some software engineers fall into the trap of copying code from Stack Overflow that solves their problem without understanding how the code actually works?
Answer: I think that “copying code” is extremely rare among stronger developers, but it seemingly must be something that happens given the number of memes that reference it. I've also seen people post that “it's faster to copy the code than to write it.” This frankly shocks me. I can't even imagine how a search for the exact bit of code that you need could possibly be faster than just writing the code. I mean, there do exist some pretty hairy algorithms that would be hard to get right in one go. And if you can't find a library, then in those rare cases starting with working code might make sense. But I'm talking a once per year kind of exceptional experience, if that. And given that I've also seen people claim that all software developers really need to know is how to iterate over lists and concatenate strings, I really doubt any of the really complex algorithms are what people are picking up. So hear's the deal: If it's faster for a developer to look up the code than to write it, what are the odds they will actually be able to fully understand it? They didn't write it, so they certainly don't understand it as well as if they did write it. One final note: A few times recently I've seen a comparison between copying and pasting code and using libraries. It's profoundly different from using a library. A library I would choose would: I think that one of the major anti-patterns common in the PHP world is to copy and paste code in preference to installing libraries. You end up with millions of copy-pasted security holes that are literally millions of times more difficult to find and fix. So no, it's not the same by any stretch. Copying code from StackOverflow is an anti-pattern. Looking at code to see how a library or method is intended to be used is fine. Looking for docs on a language is fine. I'm not against using the internet as a reference.
